note_tweet.text:
My as-of-today* AI Agent round-up:

I wanted to hate @Muse.

I love Muse. Even more so on the Power plan with Wonder behind it. It took over my personal life with its proactivity and it’s creeping upward into my professional life.

I wanted to love @OpenAI Dots.

I like Dots…okay. There’s a lot of friction and room to grow, but I see the promise. Its proactivity is misaligned (not in the “evil model” way, but in the “ is this actually helpful” way). It also needs to fix its own damned internal permissions errors that absolutely fail it every time.

I wanted to hate Grok @Bot.

I like Grok Bot. It’s helpful, but I could lose it from my stack tomorrow and be fine. The facade of running a “company” of agents falls apart when their individual “abilities” are all backed by the same model (for the most part—don’t come at me. You know what I mean.).

I wanted to love @claudeai Duet.

Claude Duet is like a brother with amnesia who doesn’t remember he’s spent the past couple of years with me. Giving this one time to cook; staying open minded.

I wanted to love @NousResearch Hermes Agent.

I found it too needy for the benefit it brought. Retired in the “Deckard” way. (Do not confuse “he’s not technical enough to use it right” (which I am) with “there’s a cost-benefit analysis to be made about how much time needed to be invested to get decent results vs the results themselves.)

*I reserve the right to change my opinion by the day with every new release.

Claude Duet is Anthropic's always-on agent bet

Anthropic opened a Claude Duet research preview on Claude Opus 5.5 — iOS, Android, and web. US Pro and Max can waitlist; Team and Enterprise are out. It runs on a cloud VM with a browser and 6,000+ connectors (Gmail, Slack, Stripe), so it keeps working while you are offline.

Here's the thing: Grok Bot shipped in August, Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots in September. Duet is that race with a tighter leash — morning brief, then pings only when a decision is needed. Payments, messages, signatures, deletes wait for a yes. Bank transfers and trades stay blocked. It polls every few hours because those checks burn the same Claude usage cap.

Always-on agents are shipping. The kill switch is the product.

#Anthropic #ClaudeDuet #AIAgents

note_tweet.text:
It's worse than that. Even if the account holder’s the only victim, being “made whole by the AI company” assumes AI agent and model providers can actually be held liable. But these companies apply terms to users of agents—who may well be the victims here—that limit what companies owe and make it hard to recover losses.

I used Claude and ChatGPT to do some research. For U.S. consumers, many companies shipping agents require binding individual arbitration and waive class actions, including Meta (Muse), OpenAI (ChatGPT / Dots), Microsoft (Copilot), Perplexity (Comet), Amazon, and Instinct. Amazon reinstated arbitration in August 2026 after previously dropping it following mass arbitration claims over Alexa.

And then we get to limits on liability. Microsoft limits recovery to one month’s service fee, or $10 for a free service. OpenAI’s cap is the greater of $100 or twelve months of fees. Meta’s Muse terms use the greater of $250 or twelve months of fees. Other providers have similar caps. This is trivial compared to potential financial losses.

Of course, some companies’ clauses do explicitly make exceptions for gross negligence or willful misconduct. But state law often limits what companies can contract away anyway, so that isn’t much of a concession. It’s going to be very hard for victims to demonstrate this, Companies will likely argue that they gave enough instructions and warnings to users and weren’t *grossly* negligent, even if they made some mistakes in how they designed agents and their guardrails.

AI companies are also putting responsibility for the agent’s actions squarely on the user. Muse’s terms say users bear the risk of financial loss from its transactions. OpenAI says users are responsible for transactions made on their behalf. The terms governing Grok expressly cover agent interactions with financial institutions and disclaim liability to the fullest extent permitted by law.

Now, Musk has said SpaceX would make Grok Bot users whole for things like inadvertent purchases or leaks in credit card information. But that promise isn’t reflected in Grok Bot’s written terms. Instead, they put responsibility on the user and exclude liability for agent actions except for losses directly caused by gross negligence or willful misconduct.

Taking this all together, the billions of dollars in financial losses scenario isn’t complicated by only whether an AI company has enough money to compensate everyone. 

The point is that if these terms are enforced, companies may be able to limit what they owe—and prevent users from bringing claims together, which is often what makes taking the case viable for plaintiffs’ lawyers.

The bottom line is that an AI company doesn’t even have to go bankrupt for victims to be left with the losses.

For someone running a business alone, there's a concrete use case. Record one product walkthrough and ask the agent to prepare short videos answering different customer questions.
